transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... people keep telling me they can't follow what I'm trying to explain anymore. Like, my artist statements and my client notes, or even just what I say in meetings. I'll be talking and I just start jumping around from the textures of the materials, straight into the budgets, and then into the secret meanings behind the pieces. 

Which, honestly, the secret meanings are the most important part. I was actually reading this article the other day about Renaissance painters and how they hid all these codes in the folds of the clothing they painted. Did you know that? They used lapis lazuli for the blue, which was so expensive they had to budget for it separately. Which kind of reminds me of how expensive groceries are getting right now. I went to buy avocados yesterday and they were almost three dollars each, it's just ridiculous. 

But, um... yeah, my clients and the gallery people just look at me like they have no idea what I'm talking about when I try to explain my work.
When did you first notice that people started having trouble following what you're saying? Was this something that started suddenly over days or weeks, or has it been going on for much longer?

Um, it wasn't sudden. It's been going on for a while now, I'd say about a year and two months? Yeah, it started right around the time I switched from community curation into full-time independent installation work. 

Community curation was just so exhausting, honestly. You have to deal with so many different personalities and local government grants. I remember this one grant application required a fifty-page proposal just to get funding for a neighborhood sculpture garden. And the paper they printed the forms on was that awful, cheap recycled paper that just drinks the ink right out of your pen. It bleeds everywhere. I only use archival ink now for my own sketches. It's waterproof, which is super important because I actually spilled coffee on my sketchbook last week and it almost ruined this drawing I was doing of a... 

Wait, I'm sorry. I lost my train of thought. But yeah, about fourteen months, ever since I went independent.
Over this past year or so, have you been feeling unusually energetic, confident, or like you need less sleep than normal? Or has your mood felt pretty much like it always does?

Um, yeah, I guess so. There are definitely these stretches where I just feel completely lit up, you know? Like I'm almost unstoppable and every single idea I have is just brilliant. I'll be working in the studio and it feels like the universe is just pouring inspiration straight into my hands. Which is funny, because I was reading about how the ancient Greeks believed in Muses, like actual entities that would come down and whisper ideas to you. I think there were nine of them? One was for astronomy, which is so interesting because I've been looking at star charts lately. The patterns are just incredible, especially if you map them out using silver leaf on dark canvas. Silver leaf is so tricky to work with, though. If you even breathe too hard, it just flies away and gets stuck to everything. I found a piece of it on my cat's nose the other day, and she just looked so regal, like a little Egyptian statue. 

But, um, where was I? Oh, right, the energy. Yeah, I get super energetic and confident, but then... I don't know, sometimes it flips. Like, a collaborator will make just a tiny comment about a piece, something really small, and I'll just snap at them. It feels way bigger than the situation warrants, just this intense irritation that bubbles up out of nowhere.
When you're in one of those 'lit up' energetic periods, how long does it typically last before your mood shifts or returns to normal? Are we talking hours, days, weeks, or longer?

Um, it's usually weeks. I'd say these energized stretches where I'm barely sleeping and just juggling way too many projects, and getting so irritable—that's been happening for about 10 months now. It's like I get locked into this high gear for weeks on end. 

Which reminds me, I actually started a new project last month that involves weaving different types of copper wire. Copper is so fascinating because of how it oxidizes. It turns that beautiful green color, like the Statue of Liberty. I visited New York once when I was in college, and the ferry ride over there was so windy I lost my favorite hat. It was this vintage wool fedora I found at a thrift store in Portland. Portland has the best thrift stores, honestly. I found this amazing mid-century modern lamp there once, but the wiring was totally shot, so I had to learn how to rewire it myself watching YouTube videos. The guy in the video had this really soothing voice, kind of like a late-night radio DJ. 

But, um... yeah, those high-energy periods definitely last for weeks at a time.
When you're not in one of those high-energy, barely-sleeping periods, what is your mood like? Do you experience periods where you feel depressed, down, or low?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I get depressed or down. When I'm not in that crazy high gear, I just feel kind of regular, I guess? Like, just normal. Which is nice, actually, because being normal means I can just sit and focus on mixing paints without feeling like I have to paint the entire room. 

I've been experimenting with mixing my own pigments lately, actually. You can buy these raw pigment powders online, and you mix them with a binder, like linseed oil or walnut oil. Walnut oil dries a lot slower, which gives you more time to work, but it smells so earthy. It reminds me of this hiking trail near my childhood home. We used to go there every autumn, and the ground would just be covered in these crushed black walnuts. They stain your hands this deep, dark brown if you touch them. My brother used to throw them at me, and I'd have stained hands for a week, which was so embarrassing in middle school. Middle school was just the worst anyway, wasn't it? Everyone is so awkward and trying to figure out who they are. I wore these terrible neon shoelaces for a whole year thinking it was a fashion statement. 

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling low. Yeah, no, I haven't really noticed feeling depressed or anything like that. Just normal.

When you're in those normal periods between the high-energy weeks, have you ever noticed times where your mood goes noticeably lower than normal—like feeling sad, hopeless, or having much less interest in things you usually enjoy?

Um, no, like I said, I don't really get sad or hopeless. When the energy stops, I'm just back to baseline, you know? Just my regular self. It's actually a relief sometimes because I can finally just sit still and read a book. I've been reading this massive biography of Frida Kahlo, actually. Her life was so intense, especially with the bus accident and everything. It's amazing how she channeled all that physical pain into her self-portraits. I tried doing a self-portrait once, but I could never get the nose right. Noses are the hardest part of the face to draw, I swear. The shading is just so subtle. You have to get the light hitting the bridge exactly right or it looks completely flat. I took this life drawing class in college where the professor made us draw the same nose for three hours straight. He was this really eccentric guy who always wore a beret, like a literal beret, indoors. Who even does that anymore? But he did teach me a lot about charcoal. Charcoal is so messy, though. You get it all over your hands and then you accidentally touch your face and you look like a chimney sweep. 

But, um... yeah, no sadness or anything like that. Just regular me.

I want to make sure I'm not missing anything. During those weeks when you're back to your normal baseline—the times when you're not in that high-energy state—have you ever had a period where your mood actually dipped below normal? Like feeling persistently sad, empty, or noticeably losing interest in art or other things you usually care about?

No, really, I promise I'm not hiding anything. When I'm not going a million miles an hour, I don't feel sad or empty or whatever. I just feel like me. I still paint, I still read, I still do my stuff. I actually just started a new painting yesterday, speaking of art. It's on this huge canvas, like four feet by four feet. I had to stretch it myself, which is such a workout. You need those special canvas pliers, and if you don't pull it tight enough, it sags in the middle like a trampoline. I used to jump on my neighbor's trampoline when I was a kid. We'd put the sprinkler under it in the summer, and it was so much fun until my sister slipped and chipped her front tooth. She had to get this fake cap put on it, and it always looked just a tiny bit whiter than the rest of her teeth. She was so self-conscious about it in high school. High school was rough for her, she was always trying to fit in with the popular crowd, but they were so mean. 

But anyway, yeah, I don't get depressed. I just go back to normal.

I want to ask about this differently. During those normal baseline weeks when you're not in the high-energy state, have you ever had stretches—even just a few days—where you felt noticeably less interested in art or your usual activities, or where things that normally bring you joy just felt kind of flat or empty?

I mean, I guess I see what you're asking, but... no, not really. Even when things feel a little quiet after all that energy, I don't feel flat. I still want to paint. Actually, I was just thinking about trying out some new brushes I got. They're made of sable hair, which is supposed to be the best for holding watercolor, but honestly, I feel a little guilty using animal hair. I was reading about how they source it, and it's kind of sad. It makes me think about my cat, Barnaby. He sheds so much I could probably make a brush out of him. He’s an orange tabby, and he has this habit of sleeping right on top of my palette if I leave it out. Last week he got cerulean blue all over his tail, and I had to chase him around the apartment with a wet towel. He hid under the sofa for hours, just glaring at me. The space under that sofa is so dusty, I really need to vacuum. I bought one of those robot vacuums, but it just gets stuck on the rug fringes and beeps until I rescue it. It’s almost more work than just sweeping. 

But um, yeah, art is always interesting to me. I don't really have days where I just don't care about it. It's always there.

During those normal weeks when you're back to baseline, have you ever noticed that you're sleeping more than usual, or that you feel more tired or sluggish than your normal self—even if you're still interested in your art?

Um, sleeping more? Not really. I mean, maybe a normal amount, like eight hours? When I'm in the high-energy weeks I barely sleep at all, so I guess compared to that it seems like a lot, but it's just regular sleeping. I don't feel sluggish or anything. I actually really like the mornings when I'm at my baseline. I make this pour-over coffee, which takes forever but it's totally worth it. You have to get the water temperature exactly right, like 205 degrees, or it burns the beans and gets all bitter. I bought this gooseneck kettle just for it. It looks like a magic lamp or something. I almost brought it to a thrift store last month because I was going through this huge minimalism phase, trying to declutter my whole apartment. I watched all those videos about only keeping things that spark joy, but then I realized basically all my art supplies spark joy, so I couldn't get rid of any of it. My closet is just overflowing with sketchbooks. I have sketchbooks from when I was like, twelve. There's this one where I tried to draw horses, but their legs look like hot dogs. It's so embarrassing. 

But yeah, my sleep is fine. I just wake up and make my coffee.

During those weeks when you're in that high-energy state—the ones lasting about 10 months now—have you ever had to miss work, cancel commitments, or have things fall apart because you were caught up in it? Or has it ever gotten so intense that you or someone close to you thought you needed to go to a hospital or see a doctor about it?

Well, I mean, it definitely affects my work. Like, I've missed some paid deadlines because I get so caught up in the ideas, and then my collaborators get really confused during meetings. I actually had an exhibition postponed recently because my notes and proposals just... stopped making enough sense for them to use. Which was really frustrating, because I had this whole vision for the gallery space. The gallery is downtown, right next to this amazing bakery that makes the best almond croissants. They have that powdered sugar on top that gets everywhere, like all over your black sweater if you're not careful. I wore a black sweater to a meeting there once and looked like I'd been rolling in snow. It was a cashmere blend, too, so it's super hard to wash. You're supposed to hand wash it with that special baby shampoo, but honestly, who has the time? I usually just lay it flat on a towel and hope for the best. 

But um, yeah, no hospital or anything like that, just... things getting a bit messed up with my art projects.

During those high-energy weeks when you're barely sleeping and full of ideas, have you ever done things that were risky or that you later regretted—like spending a lot of money impulsively, taking on way too many projects at once, or doing something that could have gotten you into trouble?

I mean, I don't think I do anything really risky. I guess I do buy a lot of art supplies when I get all those ideas, but that's just because I need them for the projects, right? Like, I went to the art supply store last week—or maybe it was a few weeks ago—and they had this massive sale on canvases. I bought so many I could barely fit them in my car. My car is this tiny little hatchback, a green one. I call it the green bean. It's getting kind of old, though, and the air conditioning smells like wet dog when you turn it on, even though I don't own a dog. I think a mouse might have lived in the vents at some point. I saw this documentary once about how mice can squeeze through holes the size of a dime. It’s terrifying if you think about it. They have collapsible skeletons or something. I bought peppermint oil because someone told me mice hate the smell of peppermint, so I just soaked some cotton balls and stuffed them in the car vents. Now the whole car just smells like a giant candy cane. It’s actually pretty intense, especially when it’s hot out. 

But um, no, I wouldn't say I do anything dangerous or get into trouble. Just... maybe buying too many canvases sometimes.
During those high-energy weeks when you're barely sleeping, do you actually feel rested and energized on just a few hours of sleep, or do you feel tired but just can't seem to sleep?

Oh, I definitely feel rested. It's actually amazing. Like, I can be up working on a piece until three in the morning, sleep for maybe two or three hours, and then I just pop awake. I feel completely bright and ready to keep going, not tired at all like I normally would be if I only got three hours. It's like my body just doesn't need it. I actually love that feeling because the mornings are so quiet. The light coming through my studio window is perfect right around 6 AM. It's this really cool, bluish light that makes all the colors on my palette look totally different. I was trying to mix this specific shade of cerulean blue the other day, and I realized I was out of titanium white, which is a disaster because you literally use titanium white for everything. I prefer the heavy body acrylics because they hold their texture so well, you know? You can get those really thick, impasto strokes that look almost like frosting. I tried baking a cake once and tried to frost it like a painting, using a palette knife and everything. It was a lemon cake. My grandmother used to make the best lemon cake, she had this secret ingredient which turned out to be just a little bit of sour cream in the batter, which keeps it super moist. 

But yeah, I don't feel tired at all during those weeks. Just energized and ready to go.

My brother used to throw them at me, and I'd have stained hands for a week, which was so embarrassing in middle school. Middle school was just the worst anyway, wasn't it? Everyone is so awkward and trying to figure out who they are. I wore these terrible neon shoelaces for a whole year thinking it was a fashion statement. 

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling low. Yeah, no, I haven't really noticed feeling depressed or anything like that. Just normal.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced distinct depressive episodes that are clearly separate from normal mood, which would support bipolar disorder (F31.6) over persistent depression with mixed features (F25.0)
doctor.question: When you're in those normal periods between the high-energy weeks, have you ever noticed times where your mood goes noticeably lower than normal—like feeling sad, hopeless, or having much less interest in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a depressive episode (sadness, hopelessness, loss of interest). My symptom profile does not include any depressive symptoms, as my diagnosis is Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type, and my mood episodes are manic/elevated without depressive episodes.

patient.answer:
Um, no, like I said, I don't really get sad or hopeless. When the energy stops, I'm just back to baseline, you know? Just my regular self. It's actually a relief sometimes because I can finally just sit still and read a book. I've been reading this massive biography of Frida Kahlo, actually. Her life was so intense, especially with the bus accident and everything. It's amazing how she channeled all that physical pain into her self-portraits. I tried doing a self-portrait once, but I could never get the nose right. Noses are the hardest part of the face to draw, I swear. The shading is just so subtle. You have to get the light hitting the bridge exactly right or it looks completely flat. I took this life drawing class in college where the professor made us draw the same nose for three hours straight. He was this really eccentric guy who always wore a beret, like a literal beret, indoors. Who even does that anymore? But he did teach me a lot about charcoal. Charcoal is so messy, though. You get it all over your hands and then you accidentally touch your face and you look like a chimney sweep. 

But, um... yeah, no sadness or anything like that. Just regular me.

inference.note: Ruled out F31.6 (bipolar disorder, currently in remission) because patient denies depressive episodes between high-energy periods and reports only 'baseline/normal' mood. The absence of depressive poles and presence of only elevated/normal mood cycling, combined with prominent flight of ideas and racing thoughts, suggests either schizoaffective disorder bipolar type (F25.0) or bipolar I disorder unspecified (F31.9). Added F31.9 as alternative given the 10-month duration of high-energy periods with decreased need for sleep and irritability, which could represent extended hypomanic or manic episodes without clear psychotic features yet established.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced distinct depressive episodes with depressed mood, anhedonia, or other depressive symptoms that would indicate bipolar disorder (F31.9) versus a primary presentation of thought disorder and disorganization consistent with schizophrenia spectrum disorder (F25.0).
doctor.question: I want to make sure I'm not missing anything. During those weeks when you're back to your normal baseline—the times when you're not in that high-energy state—have you ever had a period where your mood actually dipped below normal? Like feeling persistently sad, empty, or noticeably losing interest in art or other things you usually care about?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a major depressive episode (e.g., depressed mood, loss of interest), which are not included in my symptom profile since I have Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) without depressive episodes.

patient.answer:
No, really, I promise I'm not hiding anything. When I'm not going a million miles an hour, I don't feel sad or empty or whatever. I just feel like me. I still paint, I still read, I still do my stuff. I actually just started a new painting yesterday, speaking of art. It's on this huge canvas, like four feet by four feet. I had to stretch it myself, which is such a workout. You need those special canvas pliers, and if you don't pull it tight enough, it sags in the middle like a trampoline. I used to jump on my neighbor's trampoline when I was a kid. We'd put the sprinkler under it in the summer, and it was so much fun until my sister slipped and chipped her front tooth. She had to get this fake cap put on it, and it always looked just a tiny bit whiter than the rest of her teeth. She was so self-conscious about it in high school. High school was rough for her, she was always trying to fit in with the popular crowd, but they were so mean. 

But anyway, yeah, I don't get depressed. I just go back to normal.

inference.note: Ruled out F31.9 (Bipolar Disorder, unspecified). Patient denies depressive episodes between manic/hypomanic periods and reports returning to baseline/normal mood. This pattern is inconsistent with bipolar disorder which typically includes mood episodes below baseline. The presentation is consistent with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0): prominent flight of ideas/tangential speech, decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, irritability during high-energy periods lasting weeks, with psychotic features (magical thinking about hidden meanings, ideas of reference). No clear depressive episodes support this over bipolar disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced depressive episodes or periods of anhedonia between the high-energy manic-like states, which would help differentiate between Bipolar I Disorder (which requires depressive episodes) and other conditions like Bipolar II or cyclothymia
doctor.question: I want to ask about this differently. During those normal baseline weeks when you're not in the high-energy state, have you ever had stretches—even just a few days—where you felt noticeably less interested in art or your usual activities, or where things that normally bring you joy just felt kind of flat or empty?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a depressive episode (e.g., loss of interest, feeling empty or flat), which are not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean, I guess I see what you're asking, but... no, not really. Even when things feel a little quiet after all that energy, I don't feel flat. I still want to paint. Actually, I was just thinking about trying out some new brushes I got. They're made of sable hair, which is supposed to be the best for holding watercolor, but honestly, I feel a little guilty using animal hair. I was reading about how they source it, and it's kind of sad. It makes me think about my cat, Barnaby. He sheds so much I could probably make a brush out of him. He’s an orange tabby, and he has this habit of sleeping right on top of my palette if I leave it out. Last week he got cerulean blue all over his tail, and I had to chase him around the apartment with a wet towel. He hid under the sofa for hours, just glaring at me. The space under that sofa is so dusty, I really need to vacuum. I bought one of those robot vacuums, but it just gets stuck on the rug fringes and beeps until I rescue it. It’s almost more work than just sweeping. 

But um, yeah, art is always interesting to me. I don't really have days where I just don't care about it. It's always there.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced depressive episodes with anhedonia or other depressive symptoms that they might not be spontaneously reporting, by asking about a specific observable change in functioning during baseline periods
doctor.question: During those normal weeks when you're back to baseline, have you ever noticed that you're sleeping more than usual, or that you feel more tired or sluggish than your normal self—even if you're still interested in your art?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a depressive episode, specifically hypersomnia or fatigue/loss of energy, which are not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um, sleeping more? Not really. I mean, maybe a normal amount, like eight hours? When I'm in the high-energy weeks I barely sleep at all, so I guess compared to that it seems like a lot, but it's just regular sleeping. I don't feel sluggish or anything. I actually really like the mornings when I'm at my baseline. I make this pour-over coffee, which takes forever but it's totally worth it. You have to get the water temperature exactly right, like 205 degrees, or it burns the beans and gets all bitter. I bought this gooseneck kettle just for it. It looks like a magic lamp or something. I almost brought it to a thrift store last month because I was going through this huge minimalism phase, trying to declutter my whole apartment. I watched all those videos about only keeping things that spark joy, but then I realized basically all my art supplies spark joy, so I couldn't get rid of any of it. My closet is just overflowing with sketchbooks. I have sketchbooks from when I was like, twelve. There's this one where I tried to draw horses, but their legs look like hot dogs. It's so embarrassing. 

But yeah, my sleep is fine. I just wake up and make my coffee.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient meets criteria for bipolar I disorder (which requires at least one manic episode with marked impairment) versus bipolar II disorder (which requires hypomanic episodes without full manic severity). Specifically, I need to assess whether during those high-energy weeks, the patient experienced symptoms severe enough to cause marked impairment in functioning or require hospitalization, or whether the episodes were more moderate in severity.
doctor.question: During those weeks when you're in that high-energy state—the ones lasting about 10 months now—have you ever had to miss work, cancel commitments, or have things fall apart because you were caught up in it? Or has it ever gotten so intense that you or someone close to you thought you needed to go to a hospital or see a doctor about it?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have missed paid deadlines, confused collaborators in meetings, and had an exhibition postponed because my notes and proposals stopped making enough sense to use.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the negative impact and consequences of my symptoms on my daily life, work, and commitments, which maps directly to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, I mean, it definitely affects my work. Like, I've missed some paid deadlines because I get so caught up in the ideas, and then my collaborators get really confused during meetings. I actually had an exhibition postponed recently because my notes and proposals just... stopped making enough sense for them to use. Which was really frustrating, because I had this whole vision for the gallery space. The gallery is downtown, right next to this amazing bakery that makes the best almond croissants. They have that powdered sugar on top that gets everywhere, like all over your black sweater if you're not careful. I wore a black sweater to a meeting there once and looked like I'd been rolling in snow. It was a cashmere blend, too, so it's super hard to wash. You're supposed to hand wash it with that special baby shampoo, but honestly, who has the time? I usually just lay it flat on a towel and hope for the best. 

But um, yeah, no hospital or anything like that, just... things getting a bit messed up with my art projects.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced hypomanic or manic episodes with risky/impulsive behaviors, or if the elevated periods are characterized primarily by increased goal-directed activity and racing thoughts without significant functional impairment or poor judgment
doctor.question: During those high-energy weeks when you're barely sleeping and full of ideas, have you ever done things that were risky or that you later regretted—like spending a lot of money impulsively, taking on way too many projects at once, or doing something that could have gotten you into trouble?

patient.answer:
I mean, I don't think I do anything really risky. I guess I do buy a lot of art supplies when I get all those ideas, but that's just because I need them for the projects, right? Like, I went to the art supply store last week—or maybe it was a few weeks ago—and they had this massive sale on canvases. I bought so many I could barely fit them in my car. My car is this tiny little hatchback, a green one. I call it the green bean. It's getting kind of old, though, and the air conditioning smells like wet dog when you turn it on, even though I don't own a dog. I think a mouse might have lived in the vents at some point. I saw this documentary once about how mice can squeeze through holes the size of a dime. It’s terrifying if you think about it. They have collapsible skeletons or something. I bought peppermint oil because someone told me mice hate the smell of peppermint, so I just soaked some cotton balls and stuffed them in the car vents. Now the whole car just smells like a giant candy cane. It’s actually pretty intense, especially when it’s hot out. 

But um, no, I wouldn't say I do anything dangerous or get into trouble. Just... maybe buying too many canvases sometimes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced hypomanic or manic episodes with decreased need for sleep (not just sleeping less due to being busy, but feeling rested on significantly less sleep), which would help confirm bipolar II disorder versus other conditions with flight of ideas
doctor.question: During those high-energy weeks when you're barely sleeping, do you actually feel rested and energized on just a few hours of sleep, or do you feel tired but just can't seem to sleep?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: I can sleep two or three hours after working late and wake up feeling bright and ready to keep going, not tired the way I normally would be.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel rested and energized despite getting only a few hours of sleep, which directly corresponds to the symptom of decreased need for sleep.

patient.answer:
Oh, I definitely feel rested. It's actually amazing. Like, I can be up working on a piece until three in the morning, sleep for maybe two or three hours, and then I just pop awake. I feel completely bright and ready to keep going, not tired at all like I normally would be if I only got three hours. It's like my body just doesn't need it. I actually love that feeling because the mornings are so quiet. The light coming through my studio window is perfect right around 6 AM. It's this really cool, bluish light that makes all the colors on my palette look totally different. I was trying to mix this specific shade of cerulean blue the other day, and I realized I was out of titanium white, which is a disaster because you literally use titanium white for everything. I prefer the heavy body acrylics because they hold their texture so well, you know? You can get those really thick, impasto strokes that look almost like frosting. I tried baking a cake once and tried to frost it like a painting, using a palette knife and everything. It was a lemon cake. My grandmother used to make the best lemon cake, she had this secret ingredient which turned out to be just a little bit of sour cream in the batter, which keeps it super moist. 

But yeah, I don't feel tired at all during those weeks. Just energized and ready to go.
